items.label: text
items.text: Safety Note: Wear eye protection. Do not smell the chlorine, especially if you have asthma. Once chlorine is detected the current must be switched off.

items.label: text
items.text: We would expect to get the same volume of hydrogen as chlorine. However, in reality we appear to obtain less chlorine than expected because it is more soluble in water.

items.label: text
items.text: Not all ionic compounds can be electrolysed when they are molten. Some break up into simpler substances before their melting point. For example, copper(Il) carbonate breaks into copper(Il) oxide and carbon dioxide, even on gentle heating. It is impossible to melt it.

items.label: text
items.text: When aqueous solutions are electrolysed the products are not always the same as when molten salts are electrolysed.

items.label: section_header
items.text: PRACTICAL: INVESTIGATING THE ELECTROLYSIS OF AQUEOUS SOLUTIONS

items.label: text
items.text: We can investigate the electrolysis of an aqueous solution such as sodium chloride solution using the apparatus shown in Figure 10.6.

items.label: list_item
items.text: Figure 10.6 Electrolysis of sodium chloride solution

items.label: list_item
items.text: Set up the apparatus as shown in Figure 10.6. The glass tube, rubber bung and electrodes together are sometimes called an electrolytic cell.

items.label: list_item
items.text: Pour concentrated sodium chloride solution into the glass tube.

items.label: list_item
items.text: Place a test-tube containing sodium chloride solution over each electrode. The test-tubes must not completely cover the electrodes or ions will be unable to flow and there will be no current.

items.label: list_item
items.text: Connect the battery/powerpack to the electrodes.

items.label: list_item
items.text: The experiment should be done in a fume cupboard (fume hood) or well-ventilated room because chlorine gas is poisonous.

items.label: text
items.text: We can see if something is happening by looking for bubbles of gas or a metal forming at the electrodes. Any gases can be tested.

items.label: text
items.text: The tests for gases are covered in Chapter 18.

items.label: text
items.text: In this experiment we see bubbles of gas at both electrodes. When the gases are tested we find that hydrogen forms at the negative electrode (cathode) and chlorine forms at the positive electrode (anode).
